Drawing on interpretive flexibility within the Social Construction of Technology, this paper examines how different stakeholders understand and experience transparency in generative AI. This study draws from a global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders, and policymakers, complemented by a structured focus group with end-users, grounding the quantitative findings in qualitative insights from the group most underserved by current transparency practice. We present three key findings. First, all three groups share similar understandings of what transparency means and what it should afford, centered on ensuring accuracy and privacy. Second, gaps between the importance of transparency features and their perceived availability are substantially larger for end-users than builders, revealing how power shapes what gets built and who it serves. Only 28% of end-users report that current transparency practices reflect their needs very well, compared to 53% of builders and 49% of policymakers. Third, transparency is situationally constructed, priorities shift with context and task structure, with role-specific frames activating when context demands them and receding when it does not. We argue that meaningful AI transparency requires moving beyond a one-size-fits-all solution, including current emphases on AI disclosure and static documentation, toward pluralistic transparency infrastructures that reflect the needs of diverse users and stakeholders.

papers.title: Whose Guardrail? User Identity Shapes the Effectiveness of Model Disclaimers in Mitigating LLM Political Persuasion
papers.abstract: Politically biased AI can shift users' opinions, yet it remains unclear whether model disclaimers protect against such persuasion. We report a preregistered experiment (N=1,586) examining how disclaimer design and user characteristics shape susceptibility to politically biased AI. We varied whether disclaimers identified political bias versus potential inaccuracies and whether they included an explanation. Participants completed two decision-making tasks with an LLM biased against their political views, with outcomes assessed immediately and one week later. Disclaimers identifying political bias and including an explanation reduced persuasion, but effects varied across contexts and did not persist. Individual differences were more consistent predictors: Republicans were more persuaded and reported higher trust than Democrats across tasks. Similarly, participants who used AI more frequently were also more persuaded, whereas those with greater self-reported AI knowledge were less persuaded. These findings suggest that generic disclaimers are not enough: effective safeguards must account for user heterogeneity and context.

papers.title: False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts
papers.abstract: An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.

papers.title: Extending the MM-AR Metamodeling Platform with Process Mining Capabilities
papers.abstract: Process mining derives process models from event data recorded by information systems, but its results are usually presented as two-dimensional visualizations that are separate from the environments in which enterprise models are created and maintained. Metamodeling platforms for extended reality (XR), such as MM-AR, allow users to define modeling languages and to display models in 2D and 3D, but they do not provide access to event data or mining algorithms so far. In this paper we therefore present a first proof-of-concept for showing how an XR-based metamodeling platform can be extended with process discovery capabilities without changes to the platform core through a separate Python service based on the open source PM4Py process mining library. We demonstrate the approach using three common discovery algorithms for obtaining Petri nets and BPMN models based on CSV or XES event logs. A technical evaluation using four public event logs shows that the element counts of the created model instances match those of the PM4Py models in all 16 configurations. The integration adds between about 8 and 53 seconds per run, and this overhead grows with the size of the discovered model rather than the size of the event log. Although the prototype does not yet use the third dimension to encode process information, it established the foundations for studying such approaches.

papers.title: Better Plans, Better Outcomes: Integrating Historical Data into Student Planning in a Computing Course
papers.abstract: Effective planning is critical for academic success, but in many computing courses students often lack accurate benchmarks for assessing the difficulty and time required for academic tasks. This phenomenon is more pronounced in large courses where instructors have limited capacity to provide individualized guidance on planning and task estimation. Although many planning tools exist, still, they rarely leverage task-specific, empirically grounded data from actual course contexts. Thus, we explored whether providing task-specific, data-driven information---assignment previews and cohort-level historical statistics---could support more effective planning. We present a lightweight and data-driven planning intervention embedded in the programming assignment workflow of an undergraduate computing course. We conducted quantitative and qualitative studies with 252 students across five programming assignments. Our results indicated that, in authentic course settings, the intervention led to more conservative and executable plans, with significantly higher plan adherence. Students with stronger adherence also achieved better performance on both programming assignments and exams. Qualitative findings also showed both practical planning support and mental benefits from intervention. These results highlight the potential of data-driven intervention to support student planning in larger courses settings where individual guidance from an instructor is further limited.

papers.title: From Opinions to Commitments: Unstable Assignments and Silent Choices in AI-Mediated Proposals
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to turn citizens' opinions into collective proposals. These proposals can make assignments: who should act, what must be done, how much one should spend and by when. However, if the assignments change when the same opinions are processed again, publishing a single proposal can hide alternatives that participants never get to see. We examined this issue in four LLM mediators (three open-weight and one commercial) using opinions from DeliberationBank and Polis. For each task, a mediator drafted a proposal from thirty opinions five times, varying either the random seed or the order of the opinions. In 17% of five-run sets from the open-weight mediators and 20% from the commercial one, some runs contained assignments while others did not. Reordering the opinions changed the assignments almost as often as replacing them with opinions from different citizens. Three human annotators confirmed that the detected differences between runs were real, although the LLM judge overstated how often they occurred. Substantial variation remained under four safeguards: temperature zero, a commercial mediator, draft selection, and draft merging. The mediator's objective also shaped representation: prompts seeking agreement covered minority positions much less often than prompts asking to describe differences. A single proposal can therefore obscure choices in both the assignments it proposes and the views it excludes. We propose audits that make alternative assignments visible and disclose the objective behind each proposal.

papers.title: Haptic Shared Control for Multi-Robot Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems offer significant advantages in terms of flexibility and redundancy, enabling the efficient distribution of complex tasks among multiple robots. However, their deployment requires advanced control strategies to ensure optimal cooperation between autonomous agents and human operators. We propose a modification of the global connectivity maintenance algorithm to incorporate measurements taken in agent's local frame, using sensors with limited fields of view. This algorithm, responsible for the autonomous behavior of the multi-robot system, is combined with different adaptive supervision strategies, allowing the user to exert control at varying scales over the entire group. (i) Single Agent Control (S): The operator directly controls a single robot, (ii) Pinning Control (P): The operator imposes constraints on multiple robots to influence the group, (iii) Centroid Control (C): The operator acts on the system's center of mass to steer the entire fleet. In conjunction with the connectivity maintenance algorithm, these methods ensure compliance with inter-agent constraints while providing haptic feedback to the user regarding the system's connectivity state. The effectiveness of these approaches was evaluated through a user study, comparing performance with and without haptic feedback across multiple scenarios tailored to the different control modes.

papers.title: For You, Not for Everyone: Bystander-Aware Delivery of Critical Feedback in Robot Tutoring
papers.abstract: Robots in shared settings may expose information intended for an individual user to nearby bystanders. Robot tutoring makes this concern particularly salient: critical feedback is directed at an individual learner, yet bystanders may overhear or see it. To address this, we compared context-invariant and context-adaptive robot behaviors in a between-subjects study with 40 participants. Following an initial phase without a bystander, a bystander entered the setting. Participants then received two scripted critical feedback messages concerning their pronunciation and handwriting, independent of their actual performance. With the context-invariant behavior, the robot tutor delivered both messages aloud. With the context-adaptive behavior, the robot tutor scanned for the bystander, turned its body and display away after detecting them, gave a spoken attention cue, and presented the same feedback messages silently on its display. Participants rated the robot tutor higher in perceived privacy awareness and perceived social competence in the context-adaptive condition than in the context-invariant condition, while evidence for reduced experienced embarrassment was inconclusive. These findings inform the design and evaluation of robots that respond to bystander presence by adapting how they communicate potentially sensitive information.

papers.title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they'
papers.abstract: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.

papers.title: AI for eGovernance: Leveraging Language Technologies For Digital Inclusion
papers.abstract: The Kenyan government has invested heavily in the digitisation of public service delivery, in line with the Kenya Digital Master Plan 2022-2032. The national eGovernment platform, eCitizen, hosts services that are vital to citizens' livelihoods, including business registration, youth enterprise lending, digital literacy and tax filing. However, the platform faces digital inclusion challenges that limit equitable access for marginalised groups, particularly youth in rural areas and persons with disabilities. This exclusion is driven by a language barrier, since the platform is primarily in English with limited Swahili support, and by a text-only interface that excludes low-literacy and visually impaired users. This paper reports findings from six one-on-one interviews and an eleven-person roundtable discussion across four platforms essential to youth livelihoods: Ajira Digital, Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) iTax, Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) and the Youth Enterprise Development Fund (YEDF). Drawing on these findings, on Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 principles as a design lens for diagnosing eCitizen's accessibility gaps, and on comparator models such as Estonia's Bürokratt and India's Bhashini, the paper proposes a human-centred, systems-minded framework for embedding generative AI and language technologies into eCitizen, including text simplification, neural machine translation, text-to-speech and speech-to-text. The paper argues that, when deployed responsibly with appropriate human oversight, these interventions could meaningfully improve access to government services for linguistically excluded citizens. It also emphasises that AI alone cannot overcome the broader structural barriers, including unemployment and educational inequality, that shape digital exclusion.

papers.title: Who Is Doing the Thinking? Characterising Human Agency in First-Year Students' AI Interactions
papers.abstract: When students use generative AI to produce their work, the learning process becomes invisible. Established frameworks such as Bloom's taxonomy then classify the cognitive level of what the AI produced, not what the student contributed. We propose the Human Agency Depth Taxonomy (HADT), a preliminary six-tier taxonomy that classifies the engineering contribution a student makes in a prompt, independent of the AI's output. HADT combines three dimensions: contextual bandwidth, engineering abstraction and student agency. We applied HADT to 962 prompts from 105 students' structured AI Journals in an AI-permissive, first-year software engineering course of 145 students, and examined how agency changed over ten journalled weeks. Most prompts (84.2%) carried some student contribution beyond delegation. Agency tracked the development lifecycle. Architecture-discovery prompts dominated the requirements phase (48% of turns) and fell to 5-12% from week 9, while prompts analysing existing systems rose during build and verification (odds ratio 2.88, with turns clustered by student). Two-thirds of the variance in tier lay within students, so agency depended more on the phase of work than on the student. A turn-level rise in delegation in deadline weeks did not hold once turns were clustered by student. Explicitly specifying constraints on the AI's output was rare throughout, which we interpret as a knowledge bottleneck for novices rather than a gap in instruction. We discuss implications for course and assessment design, and for using HADT as a formative lens on how students engage with AI.

papers.title: Just Between Us? Exploring a Wearable-Mediated Channel for Discreet Human-Agent Interaction in a Shared Game Setting
papers.abstract: In shared settings, social robots may need to exchange information with an individual while limiting co-present others' access to or interpretation of that information. Publicly observable speech and gestures may not adequately support such exchanges. We investigate a wearable-mediated channel for discreet interaction that combines in-ear audio messages with deliberate rightward head tilts as responses. To examine its feasibility and participants' experiences, we studied 20 pairs (40 participants) playing a card game with a screen-based conversational agent representing a social robot, controlled by a researcher in a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Each pair played with and without the channel. One participant wore the device (the wearer), while the other (the non-wearer) was informed about the channel after gameplay. The channel conveyed information that could help the wearer or robot character select an opponent they could defeat. The information exchange and subsequent opponent selection occurred as intended in 39 of 40 channel-mediated turns. Wearers reported low perceived pressure/tension in both conditions, with no statistically significant difference between conditions, and favorable usability immediately after use. Retrospective interviews, however, revealed varied accounts of noticing the interaction among non-wearers and contrasting perceptions of teamwork and unfairness. These findings support the feasibility of wearable-mediated exchanges within this game and identify awareness and fairness as considerations for future designs.

papers.title: Making Smell Actionable in Design: Lexicon, Movement Patterns, and Gesture Cards
papers.abstract: Smell is powerful in design, yet it often remains vague and difficult to work with in studios and classrooms. While olfactory HCI has produced devices, toolkits, and scenario-based applications, designers still lack teachable, shareable resources that link smell to bodily action. This paper presents a three-phase research program that makes smell actionable by moving from lived smell experiences to movement patterns and, finally, to gesture resources. We study olfactory-motor mappings and package the results as teachable design representations through a progressively narrowing method: (1) extracting smell-verb-intent relations from user narratives; (2) capturing and clustering embodied enactments into standardized upper-limb trajectory families; and (3) translating these trajectories into gesture card representations for design teaching and ideation through design workshops. We present a three-phase translational framework and empirically derived smell-gesture correspondences that structure the smell-intent-trajectory-gesture pathway, together with reusable assets (lexicon, trajectory atlas, gesture tables, and cards) that support teaching, reuse, and adaptation across contexts.

papers.title: Setting the Stage: Enhancing Music Recommendations with Spoken Introductions to Stimulate Serendipity
papers.abstract: People like to keep their music listening fresh and interesting, but recommender systems often struggle to support this need. Even when a recommended song is potentially refreshing and enriching, listeners may not perceive it as such. Building on Silvia's appraisal theory of interest, this paper studies whether enhancing recommendations with spoken introductions, immersive or informative, can stimulate two distinct flavors of experienced serendipity: taste-broadening (sparking interest in music outside one's typical preferences) and taste-deepening (deepening interest in music within one's typical preferences). Results from a large-scale user study show that both introduction types stimulate taste-broadening and taste-deepening serendipity. Taste-broadening is most effectively stimulated through transportation (absorption in a narrative world), whereas taste-deepening is most effectively stimulated through cognitive elaboration (learning something new about the artist or the social context in which the music emerged). We discuss how these findings could be translated into practice through curated taste-broadening playlists, where both introduction types appear promising, and taste-deepening playlists, where informative introductions seem particularly effective.

papers.title: From Watching to Steering: Enabling Human-Coding Agent Collaboration through Execution Traces
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled coding agents to autonomously perform complex software development tasks, yet their long-running execution remains difficult for users to inspect, understand, and steer. We present Vibetrace, an interactive trace visualization and intervention system for agentic programming built upon OpenCode. Vibetrace introduces a human-agent collaboration paradigm of Observe, Understand, Intervene, and Evolve. It (1) visualizes agent workflows as interactive execution traces for inspecting actions, intermediate states, and failures; (2) enables users to fork execution from prior steps and provide targeted corrections without restarting validated progress; and (3) distills traces and human feedback into reusable skills for continual agent evolution. On SWE-bench Verified, distilled skills reduce input tokens by 23.0% and cost by 15.5%, while improving pass rate from 65.0% to 68.0%. User studies further demonstrate improved accuracy and efficiency over conventional log-based interaction.

papers.title: SEAM: Situated Executable Associative Memory for a Co-located Community
papers.abstract: In groups, knowledge is distributed among individuals, and how it is brought together depends on social ties. Taking inspiration from how a single mind recalls and reacts to memories and current stimulus, we build a shared memory that does this for a community, prototyped as a social app, SEAM. Members post arbitrary moments; SEAM works out how fragments relate, distills knowledge about the group, and replies in a situated and associative way. Some of these memories act as instructions that can alter how the system behaves, making it programmable by its members. We deployed SEAM to 46 people in a co-located community for two weeks of open-ended use, and ran a follow-up workshop with 14. Members shared their days, interrogated the memory, and instructed it to track routines and run games; replies introduced them to people and subjects they had never encountered. SEAM points towards communities where knowledge finds people.

papers.title: OmniScribble: Mixed-Initiative Authoring of Animated Sketches through Inspectable and Repairable AI Decisions
papers.abstract: AI-assisted creative tools reduce the effort of authoring content, but delegating creative decisions to AI can make it difficult for authors to understand, correct, or redirect work. We present OmniScribble, a system for animating multi-object sketches that treats object decomposition and motion planning as editable artifacts. Rather than generating animation end-to-end, OmniScribble presents AI proposals at verification checkpoints, where authors can accept, repair, or regenerate them. Both manual and AI-assisted authoring operate on the intermediate representation and rendering pipeline, allowing us to isolate AI delegation. In a within-subject study with eight participants, AI-assisted authoring yielded a median within-participant reduction in completion time of 71.4\%, while perceived control and motion-intent alignment remained high. Interaction traces and interviews show that participants adapted to AI errors by repairing local issues, regenerating mismatches, and accepting proposals. These findings suggest that inspectable, repairable delegation enables generative automation while maintaining control over the outcome.

papers.title: Agentic Path Maps: Exposing an Agent's Traversal Through the Garden of Forking Paths
papers.abstract: When an AI agent executes an underspecified task, it embeds choices that may contradict unarticulated user context and preferences. However, interrupting the user for clarification on all such decisions is untenable. How might agents communicate impactful, but unexplored, paths to the user after execution? To investigate, we first distill a design space for communicating alternative paths, supporting the generation of new systems and structuring dimensions of future study. We then measure the impact of one vital design space dimension on user comprehension: the number of alternatives displayed. Through a user study (n=48) in the data analysis domain, we find that participants rarely consider alternative paths of their own volition, but AI overreliance reduces when alternative paths are visualized for them. By revealing paths the agent did not take, we demonstrate how users can better interpret results and incorporate personal context.

papers.title: Palimpsestic Accountability in the US Federal AI Inventories
papers.abstract: An AI inventory is a structured, often public record in which a government or organization lists and describes the AI systems it uses or plans to use. Studies of single AI inventory releases describe what systems do but say little about how they are governed over time. We linked entries across three releases of the US Federal AI Use Case Inventory (2023--2025), compared answers only where both releases required them, and analyzed governance accounts through a dual deductive-inductive approach, guided by the Algorithmic Decision-Making Adapted for the Public Sector (ADMAPS) framework. As the inventory grew from 710 to 3,611 entries from 2023 to 2025, fewer required answers were left blank, but accountability was rewritten through three mechanisms. Each release redrew the scope of the questions; agency-assigned classifications gated what was reported; and answers were also overwritten, with gains and losses concentrated in single agencies and little account of human oversight and judgment. These findings show that each release redraws the boundary of accountability and leaves the public to re-stitch the records, a condition we term palimpsestic accountability. We recommend versioned records, reasons for every reclassification, public files that distinguish kinds of missing answers, and oversight documented as conditions to improve public sector AI accountability.

papers.title: NUISS: A User-Centered Prototype for International Student Administrative Support
papers.abstract: This study applies a streamlined User-Centered Design (UCD) approach, enhanced with AI elements, to address common administrative challenges faced by international students, such as information fragmentation and unclear processes. Using National University (NU) as a case study, the research followed core UCD stages to develop the prototype of the NU International Student Services (NUISS). These stages included task analysis informed by user stories, persona development, prototype design, and a heuristic evaluation. The high-fidelity prototype integrates three key modules-Visa Services, Certification, and Paymentwith an AI-powered assistant for proactive, personalized support. The structure is designed to enhance accessibility and minimize cognitive load. An evaluation that centered on "consistency and standards" uncovered major interface problems; this led to design refinements that boosted visual clarity and balance in a significant way. The final prototype shows that applying UCD principles in a focused way, combined with AI enhancements, can create efficient and user-friendly administrative experiences, and it offers a replicable model for similar educational contexts.

papers.title: From Embedded Finance to Embedded Obligation: A Law-and-Economics Theory of Consumer Protection in Platform-Mediated Financial Services
papers.abstract: Embedded finance is usually described as the integration of financial services into non-financial platforms. This article argues that the deeper regulatory transformation is the embedding of future legal and economic obligations into ordinary consumption, work, business, and entertainment environments. When credit, payment, wage-advance, wallet, and merchant-financing functions are delivered through plat form architecture, consumer protection cannot focus only on the formal product or licensed provider. It must also examine how obligations are framed, made salient or obscure, personalized through data, and allocated across platforms, merchants, lenders, and technical intermediaries. The article develops a law and-economics theory of Embedded Obligation Architecture, explains its irreducible object, refines its four layers, and distinguishes it from choice architecture, digital nudging, dark patterns, behavioral contract theory, and platform governance. It specifies the evidentiary limits of transferring behavioral evidence to embedded-finance contexts and proposes a Functional Embedded Obligation Test as a standard with gateway elements, evidentiary thresholds, legal vehicles, safe harbors, and proportionate remedies.

papers.title: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Korean Language Learning: Applications, Challenges, and Instructional Strategies
papers.abstract: This conceptual narrative review examines the role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in Korean language learning. The paper synthesizes recent scholarship on AI-assisted language learning, Korean language education, technology acceptance, and educational ethics to develop an analytical framework for responsible classroom use. The review focuses on four dimensions: Korean language skills, Korean-specific linguistic and cultural features, instructional design, and governance risks. The analysis suggests that generative AI can support listening, speaking, reading, and writing when tasks are explicitly designed around Korean phonology, morphology, pragmatics, and learner purposes such as TOPIK preparation, study abroad, employment, and popular-culture engagement. It also identifies challenges in cultural-pragmatic accuracy, hallucinated expressions, assessment validity, data privacy, unequal access, teacher readiness, and learner dependency. The paper concludes that generative AI should function as a mediated learning resource rather than a substitute for teachers, learner judgment, or culturally grounded interaction.

papers.title: Research on Attention Guidance and User Autonomy in AI-Powered Immersive Environments
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence gets deeply embedded into immersive environments, attention-guiding technology delivers ever more precise and efficient outcomes. Still, this improved efficiency carries an overlooked design risk: excessive AI guidance may steadily erode user agency and undermine exploratory behaviors as well as the process of meaning-making. This paper builds a critical conceptual framework to rethink attention-oriented design within AI-driven immersive settings. It defines excessive guidance and establishes theoretical links between this concept and three core facets of user agency: perceived control, voluntary choice and decision-making authority. Based on these findings, the paper calls for a paradigm shift from attention optimization to curiosity-led design. It also puts forward actionable behavioral measurement indicators covering exploration scope, average dwell time, path-following ratio, active choice frequency and recall test performance. The proposed framework supplies a new theoretical tool for human-computer interaction research in immersive scenarios and helps shift AI's role from a fixed route provider to an exploratory collaborator.

papers.title: A Study on the Mechanism and Ways to Improve New-Quality Productivity of Enterprises Driven by AI and the Digital Economy
papers.abstract: With the deep development of the digital economy and the accelerated iteration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, the formation and development of enterprise new quality productive forces have attracted increasing attention from academia and practice. Based on enterprises as the micro-subject, this paper constructs a theoretical analysis framework for the "dual-wheel drive of AI and the digital economy" and explores the formation mechanism and the path to enhancing the synergistic empowerment of enterprise these forces. The research finds that AI and the digital economy are not simply parallel drivers, but form a synergistic empowerment effect through a triple interactive mechanism of "technology-factor-organization." AI technology reshapes the technological boundary of the production function, while the digital economy reconstructs the allocation logic of production factors. The deep integration of the two drives a fundamental transformation of enterprise production modes from "factor-input-driven" to "innovation-driven". On this basis, this paper reveals the formation mechanism of these advanced productive capabilities across three dimensions: technological innovation, data element allocation, and organizational change, and proposes corresponding enhancement paths. This study has significant theoretical and practical value for understanding the micro-formation mechanism of enterprise new-quality productive forces and for guiding enterprise digital transformation and intelligent upgrading.

papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.abstract: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: Measuring Activity-Space Segregation with Multi-Source Big Data: A Physical--Digital Framework with Simulation Validation and a Real-Data Proof of Concept
papers.abstract: Segregation research increasingly measures who people encounter beyond home, yet physical mobility, place semantics, and digital activity are often combined without clear construct boundaries. This study develops a physical--digital activity-space framework that distinguishes co-presence, digital exposure, and digital interaction, and represents physical and digital segregation as separate components rather than a forced composite. Validation is deliberately split by evidentiary role. A public Washington--Baltimore Foursquare check-in subset tests the computational feasibility and robustness of a discrete group co-visitation statistic; it does not validate continuous socioeconomic exposure because the dataset lacks individual socioeconomic status. Monte Carlo experiments separately test layer-selective construct response and sensitivity to trace missingness, spatial aggregation, socioeconomic measurement error, and cross-layer coupling. The results show that the proposed calculations are executable and that the synthetic physical and digital components respond selectively to their generating mechanisms, while also revealing important measurement attenuation. No real-data estimate of income segregation, digital exposure, physical--digital coupling, or the causal effect of inequality is reported. The framework therefore combines bounded validation with a falsifiable comparative and causal research agenda.

papers.title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
papers.abstract: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-performance validation.
papers.venue: PhilPapers (PhilPapers Foundation)

papers.title: Comparison of the effects of AI-generated music on emotional responses, aesthetic enjoyment, and perceived quality between musicians and non-musicians
papers.abstract: This study investigates how emotional responses, aesthetic enjoyment, and perceived quality elicited by artificial intelligence (AI)-generated music differ between musicians and non-musicians using a mixed-methods research design. To conceptualize the effects of technological mediation on musical experience, the study adopts a multilayered theoretical framework encompassing Meyer's theory of musical emotion, Huron's expectation model, the Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS), Bourdieu's theory of cultural capital, and Benjamin's concept of mechanical reproducibility. The study included a total of 64 participants, consisting of 32 musicians and 32 non-musicians. Data were collected using the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS), the Geneva Emotional Music Scale (GEMS), and the Toronto Empathy Questionnaire (TEQ), while the qualitative dimension was enriched through semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions. Descriptive statistics indicated that AI-generated music produced moderate levels of emotional arousal and aesthetic enjoyment. MANOVA and post hoc multiple comparison analyses revealed that non-musicians reported significantly higher levels of pleasure (M = 4.12) than musicians (M = 3.24), whereas the opposite pattern was observed for inspiration. Among musicians, a positive correlation was found between pleasure and inspiration (r = .284), while a negative correlation emerged among non-musicians (r = −.357). Qualitative findings indicated that although AI-generated music was perceived as technically impressive, emotional engagement remained limited due to a perceived lack of authenticity. While musicians appreciated its technical compositional competence, they adopted a more critical stance regarding emotional depth. In contrast, non-musicians reported greater aesthetic pleasure but experienced lower levels of creative inspiration. These findings are consistent with theoretical perspectives concerning cultural capital and the social construction of aesthetic judgment.

papers.title: Video and digital games: Historical controversies, benefits, and risks for children and adolescents
papers.abstract: Video and digital games have been the focus of sustained public and scientific debate since their commercial emergence in the late 1970s, particularly regarding their effects on children and adolescents. Early public and scientific discourse frequently portrayed gaming as a source of physical injury, addiction, aggression, social isolation, academic problems, and moral decline. However, subsequent empirical research has produced a substantially more differentiated picture of both the benefits and risks of gaming. This review examines the historical foundations of controversies surrounding video and digital games and synthesizes contemporary evidence concerning their cognitive, emotional, social, therapeutic, and physical effects. . Research indicates that moderate, purposeful gaming may improve visuospatial abilities, attentional control, problem-solving, mood regulation, social connection, and selected educational outcomes. Gaming-based interventions have also demonstrated therapeutic potential, particularly for depressive symptoms and attention-related difficulties among young people. At the same time, important risks remain, especially when gaming becomes excessive, compulsive, or disruptive to everyday functioning. These include repetitive-strain injuries, sleep disruption, problematic gaming, and adverse mental-health and academic outcomes. Evidence concerning violent games and serious real-world aggression remains more contested, with recent research emphasizing relatively small effects and the importance of individual and contextual factors. Overall, the evidence suggests that the developmental consequences of gaming for children and adolescents depend less on gaming itself than on the duration, content, context, and pattern of engagement.

papers.title: Screen use in children and adolescents: Developmental risks, benefits, and educational implications
papers.abstract: The “war against screens” — the intense parental and societal pushback against children’s and adolescents’ excessive use of smartphones, social media, tablets, and games — was lost from the outset. Modern life is inseparable from screens; even closed communities fail at total prohibition. Cross-national parent movements (Wait Until 8th, Smartphone Free Childhood) and policy responses (age restrictions, phone-free schools in Australia, Brazil, Europe, etc.) reflect these worries. Practical guidance centers on the Surgeon General’s “5 Ds” (Discuss, Do, Delay, Divert, Disconnect) and family media plans rather than prohibition. Historical roots of techno-skepticism are traced to Weizenbaum (1976) and Dreyfus. Part 2 focuses on doomscrolling (“catastrophe scrolling”) – compulsive consumption of distressing news. Evolutionary negativity bias, amygdala activation, and dopamine loops sustain the behavior. Gifted adolescents are particularly vulnerable due to intellectual hyperarousal, high empathy, and still-maturing self-regulation. Preliminary group interventions using gradual behavior shaping show promise in reducing the habit. Part 3 dismantles the popular notions of “brain rot” (Oxford Word of the Year 2024) and Spitzer’s “digital dementia.” Neither is a clinical entity; rigorous evidence for permanent cognitive atrophy from screen use is lacking. Content and context matter far more than the medium itself. Paradoxically, technology use in older adults is associated with lower cognitive-decline risk. Both terms remain useful only as red flags for problematic, addictive patterns that impair sleep, mood, and functioning. Overall, screens cannot be eliminated, but intentional limits, high-quality content, protected sleep, real-world activities, parental modeling, and platform accountability can substantially mitigate risks. The goal is not victory in a lost war, but wiser coexistence.

papers.title: Kindergarten Teachers’ Perceptions of Instructional Approaches for Teaching Sequencing Concepts: Worksheet, Hands-On, and BeeBot-Integrated Lessons
papers.abstract: The purpose of this qualitative multiple-case study was to explore kindergarten teachers’ perceptions of three instructional approaches for teaching sequencing concepts: worksheet-based instruction, hands-on manipulative instruction, and BeeBot-integrated instruction. Sequencing is a foundational early literacy skill that supports reading comprehension, story retelling, and understanding the order of events. Although sequencing is commonly taught through traditional instructional methods, limited research has examined how kindergarten teachers perceive the use of educational robotics as a tool for literacy instruction. The study was guided by constructivist theory, sociocultural theory, and developmental systems theory. Participants included six kindergarten teachers from a public elementary school in Alabama, with each teacher serving as an individual case within the multiple-case study design. Data were collected through pre-interviews, written reflections, and post-interviews, following the implementation of three sequencing lessons representing the instructional approaches under investigation. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, beginning with within-case analysis of each teacher’s data through open coding and categorization of codes, followed by cross-case analysis to identify patterns, similarities, differences, and overarching themes across the six cases. Five major themes emerged from the analysis. First, teachers perceived hands-on and BeeBot-integrated instruction as increasing student engagement compared to worksheet-based instruction. Second, teachers reported that BeeBots promoted collaboration, communication, and problem-solving among students. Third, participants identified unique instructional benefits associated with each approach, including independent practice through worksheets, active learning through hands-on activities, and critical thinking through BeeBot-integrated instruction. Fourth, implementation was influenced by factors such as preparation time, resource availability, technology access, and teacher support. Fifth, teachers reported intentions to increase their use of interactive and technology-supported sequencing instruction in future literacy teaching. Taken together, the findings indicate that kindergarten teachers perceive sequencing instruction as a balanced integration of traditional, hands-on, and technology-supported learning experiences rather than reliance on a single instructional approach. Participants perceived BeeBot-integrated and hands-on instruction as enriching literacy learning by increasing engagement, collaboration, and higher-order thinking, while recognizing that traditional worksheet-based activities continue to serve important instructional purposes. Overall, the study suggests that educational robotics are most valuable when thoughtfully integrated into developmentally appropriate literacy instruction and supported through adequate planning, resources, and professional learning. These findings contribute to the growing body of research on educational robotics in early childhood education and offer practical implications for literacy instruction, teacher preparation, and technology integration in kindergarten classrooms.

papers.title: Weathering the Divide: Social Determinants, Neighborhood Context, and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Among African American Women
papers.abstract: Background: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) disproportionately affects African American women and contributes to racial health disparities in the United States. Although genetic susceptibility influences disease risk, growing evidence suggests that social determinants of health (SDOH), including neighborhood conditions, structural racism, and socioeconomic disadvantage, contribute to disease development and progression. Epigenetic mechanisms may provide a biological pathway linking adverse social conditions to chronic disease disparities. This dissertation examined the influence of SDOH on SLE disparities through evidence synthesis and empirical investigation to inform public health practice and policy. Methods: This integrated learning experience consisted of three complementary manuscripts. Aim 1 was a PRISMA-ScR scoping review examining associations among SDOH, epigenetic mechanisms, and chronic disease outcomes. Aim 2 was a secondary cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from a case-control study the Social Factors, Epigenomics, and Lupus in African American Women (SELA) Study examining neighborhood racial composition and SLE disease activity using generalized estimating equations (GEE). Aim 3 was a secondary case-control analysis of SELA data examining neighborhood racial composition and confirmed SLE diagnosis using GEE. Results: Aim 1: Twenty-two studies demonstrated associations between adverse SDOH, epigenetic alterations, and chronic disease outcomes. Neighborhood disadvantage, economic instability, food insecurity, adverse childhood experiences, and discrimination were associated with accelerated biological aging and poorer health outcomes, whereas educational attainment, social capital, supportive relationships, and neighborhood resources were protective. Aim 2: Neighborhood racial composition was not associated with SLE disease activity after adjustment for age and educational attainment; however, lower educational attainment was associated with greater disease activity. Aim 3: Neighborhood racial composition was associated with confirmed SLE diagnosis after adjustment for age, educational attainment, and Sea Islander status. Each one-percentage-point increase in neighborhood African American composition was associated with approximately 2.3% higher odds of SLE diagnosis. Conclusions: Adverse SDOH contribute to chronic disease disparities through individual- and neighborhood-level pathways. Neighborhood racial composition was associated with SLE diagnosis but not disease activity, suggesting neighborhood context may influence disease occurrence more than disease severity. These findings support public health policies and community interventions that address structural inequities and neighborhood disadvantage to reduce SLE disparities among African American women.

papers.title: Pieces Solving a Puzzle: Emerging Roles and Cross-Field Analogies During a Distributed Epistemic Game
papers.abstract: In an effort to describe why some problems can’t be solved, a character compared them to a cubic meter of platinum - a block so dense that all the people who could squeeze around it still couldn’t lift it off the ground. In the same way, these problems simply can’t have enough people gathered around and communicating about them - and so they remain unsolved. This research looks at the first Polymath Project (2009) as an example of a distributed epistemic game to examine how groups engage with complex problems. and without a locally omniscient individual. In this setting of epistemic uncertainty, interactions between individuals reveal patterns of participation, and an analogy opens a new solution pathway by introducing a problem-solving approach from another field. These insights answer the initial question of the Polymath Project - ‘Is massively collaborative mathematics possible?’ - and offer hope for lifting the cubic meter of other unsolvable problems.

papers.title: Development and Psychometric Evaluation of the Digital Native Identity Scale among Upper Secondary School Students in Tehran
papers.abstract: Objective: The present study aimed to develop and analyze the psychometric properties of the Digital Native Identity Scale among upper secondary school students in Tehran. Methods and Materials: This study employed an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design and was conducted in two qualitative and quantitative phases. In the qualitative phase, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 24 experts in educational sciences, psychology, sociology, and information technology. Thematic analysis was used to identify the dimensions and components of digital native identity, based on which a 21-item scale comprising six dimensions was developed. In the quantitative phase, data were collected from 402 students, including 206 girls and 196 boys, who were selected through multistage cluster sampling. The data were analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis, Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega coefficients, and the graded response model within the framework of item response theory. Findings: The findings indicated that the six-factor model was confirmed with satisfactory goodness-of-fit indices (CFI = 0.942, TLI = 0.935, RMSEA = 0.054, and SRMR = 0.047), and all factor loadings ranged from 0.63 to 0.81. The reliability coefficients for the total scale (α = 0.91 and ω = 0.93) and the reliability coefficients for its dimensions, which ranged from 0.78 to 0.86, indicated excellent internal consistency. The graded response model analysis showed that 17 of the 21 items demonstrated an adequate fit to the model. The item discrimination parameters ranged from 1.56 to 2.12, indicating good to excellent discrimination. The information functions confirmed that the scale provided high levels of information across a broad range of the latent trait continuum. Differential item functioning analysis by gender showed that only one item exhibited minor DIF, indicating that the scale was essentially free from gender bias. Furthermore, comparison of the unidimensional and multidimensional item response theory models demonstrated the significant superiority of the multidimensional model. Conclusion: Based on the findings, the Digital Native Identity Scale possesses satisfactory validity, reliability, and measurement information and can be used as a valid instrument for assessing different dimensions of identity formation among Iranian adolescents.

papers.title: Teacher Technology Adoption and Pedagogical Integration: Digital Competence, Institutional Support, and Student Engagement
papers.abstract: Digital technology integration requires teachers to combine technological competence with pedagogical knowledge and supportive institutional conditions. This study reviews literature on teacher technology adoption, digital competence, pedagogical integration, institutional support, and student engagement in secondary education. The synthesis identifies teacher-level, technological, and institutional factors that shape technology adoption and influence the transition from basic digital use to pedagogically meaningful integration. An integrated framework is developed to explain how teacher competence, perceived usefulness, infrastructure, leadership support, professional development, and instructional alignment interact in technology-supported teaching. Student engagement is positioned as a potential educational outcome of purposeful pedagogical integration rather than a direct consequence of technology availability.

papers.title: Integrating Student-Mined Data In Youth Computer Science Learning: An Investigation Of Learning Outcomes And Educational Strategies
papers.abstract: As data increasingly shapes participation in society, there is growing emphasis on preparing youth to engage with data through computer science education. Existing K-12 computing and data science curricula have expanded opportunities for learners to analyze and interpret data; however, many learning experiences continue to rely on datasets and inquiry structures designed by others, limiting authentic engagement, personal relevance, and learner agency. This dissertation investigates the integration of student-mined data in youth computer science learning and examines its influence on computational thinking, epistemic agency, and learning experiences among high school students. Using a qualitative approach, data collected from youths of high school age provide insights into educational strategies that support participation, agency, and knowledge construction in computing contexts. Findings revealed four major themes: (1) student-mined data connected learning to students' communities and lived experiences, increasing engagement and relevance; (2) participation in student-mined data activities strengthened computational thinking through authentic data collection, analysis, and interpretation; (3) students demonstrated greater interest, motivation, and ownership of their learning when investigating personally meaningful datasets; and (4) student-mined data fostered epistemic agency by positioning learners as active producers of knowledge rather than passive consumers. These findings suggest that culturally relevant, student-driven data inquiry can enhance both technical and cognitive learning outcomes in computer science education.

papers.title: Enhancing 21st-Century Learning Skills in Early Childhood through a Local Wisdom-Integrated Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics (STEAM) Learning Package to Support Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): A Bibliometric and Mixed-Methods Study
papers.abstract: This study examined the effect of a local wisdom-integrated science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics (STEAM) learning package on 21st-century learning skills in early childhood and positioned the topic within Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)-oriented education through bibliometric mapping. 40 early childhood students participated in the “Rice and Farmers” learning unit using the I-WISDOM package. Quantitative data were analyzed using dependent sample t-tests and Cohen’s effect size, while qualitative data were interpreted through analytic description. The findings showed significant improvement in creativity, problem solving, communication, and collaboration. Students also demonstrated appreciation of rice farming as local wisdom. The study supports quality education, cultural sustainability, and early skill development through STEAM-based learning.

papers.title: Enhancing Design Thinking through Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Augmented Curriculum to Support Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in Chinese Vocational Education: A Bibliometric and Mixed-Methods Study
papers.abstract: Traditional vocational art and design education in China often emphasizes technical skills while providing limited support for creative problem-solving. This study developed and evaluated an artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented curriculum to enhance design thinking and support Sustainable Development Goals in Chinese vocational education. A bibliometric and mixed-methods design was applied through curriculum mapping, pre-test and post-test measurement, and semi-structured interviews. The findings showed improvement in overall design thinking, especially collaboration, problem orientation, and test iteration. However, empathy developed more slowly because generative AI produced standardized outputs with limited emotional depth. The study highlights the value of integrating AI with human guidance, reflective practice, and ethical creative judgment.

papers.title: Developing a Mathematics Instructional Model to Enhance Computational Thinking Skills among Pre-service Mathematics Teachers in Support of the Sustainable Development Goals: A Bibliometric Analysis and Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Computational thinking is essential for preparing future mathematics teachers to address complex problems in digital and sustainable education. This study developed and evaluated a mathematics instructional model for pre-service mathematics teachers using a descriptive bibliometric analysis and an empirical research-and-development approach. Scopus data showed rapid growth in publications on computational thinking from 1987 to 2025, confirming its increasing educational relevance. The model comprised six stages: situation presentation, analysis, association, synthesis, designing and arranging problem-solving procedures, and conclusion. 30 participants completed a one-group pretest-posttest implementation. Results showed significant improvements in decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithm design, supported by positive interview responses. The model provides a framework for computational thinking development and supports SDG-oriented quality teacher education.

papers.title: Fragmented Systems to Integrated Digital Transformation: An Enterprise Architecture Model for Indonesian Private Higher Education
papers.abstract: Digital transformation in private higher education requires the integration of institutional strategy, governance, people, information systems, and technology. However, many Indonesian Private Higher Education Institutions (PTS) still experience fragmented information systems, limited data integration, weak business-IT alignment, and the absence of a contextual architectural blueprint. This study develops an Enterprise Architecture for Digital Transformation (EADT) model for Indonesian PTS. A Design Science Research approach was used through problem identification, framework analysis, component synthesis, contextual analysis, model development, and expert validation. Enterprise Architecture and Digital Transformation components were identified and mapped against factual institutional needs and transformation barriers. The resulting model integrates strategic, business, information, technology, governance, human, and digital-capability dimensions within a hierarchical architecture. The EADT model provides a contextual framework for aligning institutional objectives with digital-transformation implementation in Indonesian private higher education.

papers.title: A DIALOGUE-BASED DECISION-MAKING SYSTEM FOR SOLVING PLANNING PROBLEMS UNDER UNCERTAINTY
papers.abstract: Decision-making process is characterized by the need to resolve complex, multi-criteria issues. Decisions in fields such as economics, logistics, healthcare, industry, and public administration are frequently made under conditions of uncertainty. The incomplete, imprecise, or volatile nature of data directly impacts the quality of these decisions. In this context, dialogue-based decision-making systems create opportunities for more efficient planning by combining the user's knowledge and experience with intelligent algorithms. This article examines the application of dialogue-based decision-making systems for solving planning problems under conditions of uncertainty. In modern intelligent systems, the processing of uncertain data, the management of user interaction, and the making of optimal decisions are of significant importance. Dialogue systems facilitate interactive collaboration with the user to evaluate various alternatives, analyze risks, and ensure the selection of the most suitable decision. The article analyzes the design principles, advantages, and application areas of such systems.

papers.title: ENGINEERED ACOUSTIC FEATURES AND NEURAL NETWORKS FOR MUSIC EMOTION RECOGNITION: AN EMPIRICAL COMPARISON ON THE DEAM DATASET
papers.abstract: This study compares engineered acoustic features with spectrogram based convolutional neural networks for static Valence and Arousal prediction on the 1,802-song DEAM dataset. Random Forest and XGBoost use 520 dimensional openSMILE features, while the CNN learns from 30-second log-mel spectrograms. The evaluation uses five saved song-level train, validation, and test partitions. The original XGBoost baseline achieves mean RMSE of 0.780 for Valence and 0.793 for Arousal, below every tested CNN configuration on both targets in all five runs. Increasing the CNN to 101,506 parameters lowers its mean RMSE to 0.837 and 0.855, respectively; a further increase to 403,714 parameters gives little additional benefit. A ten-configuration sweep for each tree model places the original settings among several competitive choices. Auxiliary analyses examine feature importance, prediction averaging, and linear recalibration. These results support openSMILE features with XGBoost as a practical baseline for this song-level prediction task.

papers.title: DYNAMICS OF PORTFOLIO ASSESSMENT STRATEGY IN EVALUATING THE ENGLISH LANGUAGE SKILLS FOR PUPILS WITH HEARING IMPAIRMENTS IN FAKO DIVISION, SOUTH WEST REGION OF CAMEROON
papers.abstract: This study examined the impact of portfolio assessment on evaluating the English language skills of pupils with hearing impairment in Fako Division, Cameroon. Portfolio assessment, as an informal and learner-centred approach, was explored within the framework of inclusive education, where traditional assessment methods often fail to adequately reflect the abilities of learners with hearing loss. The research utilised a quasi-experimental design involving pupils with hearing impairment in selected inclusive primary schools. Data were gathered through English language tests, classroom observations, and interviews with parents, teachers, head teachers, and the divisional delegate. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, and regression analysis, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. The results indicated that pupils subjected to portfolio assessment performed significantly better in English language skills than those assessed through conventional methods. Statistical analysis (SPSS t-tests and regression) showed that pupils assessed via portfolios scored notably higher on post-tests (portfolio group mean=12.78 versus control=11.14; t(38)=2.919, p<.05). Regression analysis demonstrated that portfolio use was a strong predictor of language improvement (β=0.336, p<.001). Classroom observations and interview findings further revealed that portfolio assessment encouraged ongoing learning, increased learner engagement, self-reflection, and heightened teacher awareness of individual progress. The study concludes that portfolio assessment is an effective method for evaluating the English language skills of pupils with hearing impairment and recommends its systematic adoption within inclusive classroom practice.

papers.title: Algorithmic Justice and Responsible AI Journalism: A Comparative Communication Policy Perspective in East Asia
papers.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence and automated content curation rapidly reshape the global media landscape, the intersection of algorithmic justice and media governance has become a critical frontier for sustainable development. This study provides a comparative communication policy analysis of China and South Korea, focusing explicitly on how their distinct regulatory toolkits address the tension between algorithmic fairness and platform accountability in AI journalism. While China utilizes a top-down, state-centric regulatory framework emphasizing ideological security, algorithmic registration, and strict synthetic media labeling, South Korea employs a multi-stakeholder co-regulation model driven by personal data protection, anti-monopoly platform intervention, and civil society oversight. Through a detailed textual analysis of key policy documents—including China's Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations and South Korea's Guidelines for AI Service Ethics to Protect Users—alongside empirical evidence from prominent algorithmic news curation platforms (Toutiao and Naver), this paper evaluates the implementation efficacy and structural trade-offs of each nation's approach. We demonstrate that while both models mitigate the risks of digital infodemics and algorithmic bias, they face contrasting trade-offs between regulatory efficiency and editorial independence. Finally, this study introduces the "Policy-Media-Society" (PMS) responsive governance framework, clarifying how systemic institutional adaptations can advance UN Sustainable Development Goal 16 (SDG 16) by ensuring public access to transparent, verified information.

papers.title: From Legal Databases to AI-Assisted Justice: A Risk-Sensitive Framework for the Application of Information Technologies in Law
papers.abstract: This paper analyzes information technologies in law and proposes a risk-sensitive framework for responsible digital legal practice. Using EU regulatory developments as the main legal lens, while also referring to international standards and policy materials, the study reviews legal databases, case-management systems, artificial intelligence and natural language processing, electronic identification and signatures, digital evidence, online dispute resolution and electronic courts. The paper's contribution is to connect general principles of transparency, human oversight, source verification and accountability to concrete stages of legal work: intake, research, drafting, identity assurance, signing, archiving and audit. Brief examples of AI-assisted drafting, online dispute resolution and electronic signature verification illustrate the practical use of the framework. The analysis concludes that digital legal systems create value when they remain traceable, proportionate and subject to professional responsibility rather than replacing legal judgment.

papers.title: A Study on the Cultural Resource Value Assessment of Min School Guqin and Cultural Creative Product Development Based on PEST Theory
papers.abstract: Taking the Min School (Pucheng School) Guqin as the research object, this paper designs a cultural resource value evaluation scale under the PEST theoretical framework, collects first-hand data via questionnaire survey, and performs descriptive statistics, reliability test, exploratory factor analysis and correlation analysis with SPSS to quantitatively evaluate the cultural resource value of the Min School Guqin. The study finds that the Min School Guqin has notable strengths in policy support and technology application, yet faces practical challenges including insufficiently unleashed market consumption demand and low audience participation. Based on empirical findings, this paper proposes targeted cultural and creative product development strategies from political, economic, social and technological dimensions, so as to provide practical references for the living inheritance and industrial development of the Min School Guqin, as well as methodological insights for value evaluation and development of similar intangible cultural heritage (ICH) resources.

papers.title: Antitrust Regulation of Algorithmic "Platform-Driven Involution'': From Governing the Corporate Person to Governing the Platform Ecosystem
papers.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly govern competition through algorithmically administered rules that allocate visibility, subsidies, commissions, participation opportunities, and sanctions. This article reconstructs ``platform-driven involution'' as a testable, portfolio-based theory-of-harm framework rather than a freestanding antitrust offense. Its application remains anchored in market definition, dominance, identified conduct under Article 22 of China's Anti-Monopoly Law, causal proof, competitive effects, and objective justification. The article clarifies that ecosystem analysis supplements rather than replaces relevant-market analysis and develops an evidence architecture for separating platform-induced effects from macroeconomic, demand, cost, and merchant-specific confounders. It then distinguishes preventive measures already supported by Chinese hard law or voluntary compliance guidance from compulsory competition-specific filing and pre-deployment assessment that would require clearer future authorization. The 2026 Trip.com decision is used to show how traffic allocation, exclusivity, lowest-price requirements, technical monitoring, and sanctions can form an integrated abuse architecture while liability remains tied to established statutory categories. Comparative analysis of EU platform regulation and Google Shopping supports calibrated procedural prevention, meaningful explanation, and causal discipline without protecting inefficient competitors or condemning aggressive competition.

papers.title: From Chopin to Kitsch? Pauline Viardot's Vocal Mazurkas and the popularisation of classical music
papers.abstract: This article examines the concept of ‘popular music’ in the context of the work of Frédéric Chopin (1810–1849). The paper analyses six mazurkas by the Polish composer and their transcription for voice and piano, performed by the opera diva Pauline Viardot (1821–1910) to words by the French poet Louis Pomme (1831–1901). This chamber vocal cycle, composed by Viardot, illustrates the established poetics of the salons of the second third of the 19th century, where literature and music converged. Based on an analysis of various sources, this study examines the history of the works’ creation, their imagery and intonation, as well as the harmonic features of these vocal miniatures, whilst reconstructing their context. As a result, a connection is revealed between Viardot’s vocal mazurkas and Chopin’s songs, composed between 1829 and 1847, in the themes of love and loneliness. The aim of this article is to investigate how the opera singer bridges the gap between classical music and the mass audience and becomes a creator of kitsch. The research methodology includes an analysis of historical sources, as well as a musical and literary analysis of Chopin’s and Viardot’s mazurkas. The author concludes that kitsch emerges at the intersection of classical and popular music, where the integration of various elements from different mazurkas helps Viardot achieve a precise correspondence between the expressive content of the text and Chopin’s musical language.

papers.title: CRYPTOCURRENCY REGULATION: A DESCRIPTIVE CASE STUDY ON THE POLICIES OF INDIA, VIETNAM, AND THE REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES
papers.abstract: AbstractThe impact of cryptocurrency on the global economy is enormous. It has brought about changes both positive and negative. However, the advantages of cryptocurrency are far-reaching for many of its users who experience financial and economic inequality, causing its prevalence in lower-middle income countries. This development has caused the governments in these countries to tackle the complicated legal implications that follow. This paper aims to examine the regulatory trajectories and compile the legislation put in place in the countries of India, Vietnam and the Republic of Philippines and how each country has reckoned with this asset. papers.title: CREATIVE LEADERSHIP AS A COGNITIVE-SOCIAL BUFFER AGAINST RUMINATION AND ORGANIZATIONAL ANOMIE: THE FULL MEDIATION ROLE OF EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE AND EMOTIONAL CAPACITY
authors: DR. S. ANTONY RAJ AISHWARYA ANANDAVALLI MN
papers.abstract: Purpose – This study aims to investigate the full mediation effect of Creative Leadership (CL) in the relationship between employee Emotional Capacities (Emotional Contagion (EC), Emotional Intelligence (EI), and Emotion Regulation (ER)) and two critical forms of psychological strain: Rumination (R) and organizational Anomie (A). The research addresses the gap in understanding the specific psychological mechanism through which positive leadership prevents both individual cognitive dwelling and systemic organizational malaise. Design/methodology/approach – A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed using a structured, self-administered survey. Data were collected from $N=350$ working professionals. Hypotheses were tested using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), with analysis conducted using SPSS and LISREL. Findings – The proposed structural model achieved an outstanding fit (RMSEA = 0.003). Emotional Contagion (beta = 1.42) was confirmed as the strongest positive predictor of perceived Creative Leadership. Crucially, CL acts as a significant negative buffer against both Anomie (beta = -0.34) and Rumination (beta = -0.29). The results confirmed that CL fully mediates the relationship between employee emotional capacities and strain outcomes. Research limitations/implications – The study's main limitation is its cross-sectional design, which restricts definitive causal inference. Practically, the findings imply that organizations should integrate emotional resonance into CL training to leverage the strong predictive power of Emotional Contagion. Future work should utilize longitudinal designs or test moderators to confirm the causal sequence and explore contextual variations. Originality/value – This paper provides a novel, empirically-validated framework quantifying CL’s role as a cognitive-social buffer against both individual (R) and organizational (A) strain. It uniquely establishes the paramount role of Emotional Contagion as the primary antecedent for effective Creative Leadership perception, refining leadership theory.
